reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer / NCCN genetic/familial guidelines
clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic germline pathogenic variants in MUTYH, and unusually among the hereditary polyposis syndromes it is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
MUTYH encodes a base-excision-repair glycosylase that corrects oxidative DNA damage, so its loss leads to characteristic somatic mutations, notably in the APC and KRAS genes
Typically presents with attenuated colorectal polyposis of tens to low hundreds of adenomas, though serrated and hyperplastic polyps also occur, with a high colorectal cancer risk
The phenotype can closely mimic attenuated familial adenomatous polyposis, but the recessive inheritance pattern helps distinguish the two
Extracolonic features include duodenal adenomas and an increased risk of duodenal and other cancers, so upper gastrointestinal surveillance is warranted
Management centres on colonoscopic surveillance with polypectomy, with risk-reducing colectomy reserved for uncontrollable polyp burden or cancer
Two common founder variants account for many cases in populations of European ancestry, but comprehensive gene analysis is needed to detect all pathogenic changes
reference.pathophysiology: MUTYH encodes a DNA glycosylase that is part of the base-excision-repair system responsible for correcting the mutagenic effects of oxidative DNA damage. When both alleles carry loss-of-function variants, the enzyme can no longer remove adenines misincorporated opposite the oxidised guanine lesion 8-oxoguanine, so characteristic G-to-T transversions accumulate. These mutations preferentially strike growth-regulatory genes such as APC and KRAS, driving adenoma formation through the same adenoma-carcinoma sequence seen in other colorectal polyposis syndromes.
additionalDifferentials: Familial adenomatous polyposis and its attenuated form
additionalInvestigations: Germline MUTYH sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis to confirm biallelic variants
Colonoscopy with polypectomy and histological characterisation of polyps
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal assessment
APC germline testing to exclude adenomatous polyposis when phenotype overlaps
Full blood count and iron studies for occult blood loss
Family testing that considers both parents given recessive inheritance
redFlags: A discrete or advanced colorectal lesion suggesting malignancy
Advanced-histology duodenal adenoma on upper endoscopy
Iron-deficiency anaemia or overt gastrointestinal bleeding
Rapid change in polyp burden between surveillance examinations
reference.prognosis: With regular colonoscopic surveillance and polypectomy the colorectal cancer risk can be substantially reduced, and prognosis is favourable when disease is detected early. Because risk persists lifelong and extends to the duodenum, ongoing surveillance and, where required, surgical management remain important.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the condition as dominant and failing to test both parents and siblings appropriately
Diagnosing attenuated familial adenomatous polyposis without excluding biallelic MUTYH variants
Detecting only a single founder variant and wrongly concluding the diagnosis is excluded
Neglecting upper gastrointestinal surveillance for duodenal disease
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
NCCN Guidelines: Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment - Colorectal
management: MAP is a hereditary polyposis syndrome managed by lifelong cancer-risk reduction rather than cytotoxic or targeted cancer therapy
Attenuated polyposis with a manageable adenoma count is managed with colonoscopic surveillance and polypectomy to clear polyps as they arise

Polyp burden that cannot be reliably cleared endoscopically, or a confirmed colorectal cancer, warrants consideration of risk-reducing colectomy or proctocolectomy, individualised to polyp distribution, rectal sparing, age, and preference

Established colorectal cancer in a MAP patient is staged and treated per standard colorectal cancer principles for that stage, including surgical resection with or without adjuvant chemotherapy for node-positive or high-risk disease; no MAP-specific systemic regimen is implied
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal examination is warranted given the increased duodenal cancer risk
Advanced-histology duodenal adenomas found on surveillance should prompt closer endoscopic follow-up or endoscopic/surgical resection depending on size and grade
MAP carries an increased gastric cancer risk alongside other familial syndromes, so gastric screening should be guided by a genetics/GI guideline

Overall approach follows an escalation ladder: surveillance and polypectomy first, escalating to segmental or extended colectomy when polyp burden outstrips endoscopic control, and to standard-of-stage cancer treatment if invasive cancer develops
Lifelong colonoscopy at intervals appropriate to prior polyp findings, plus periodic upper endoscopy with duodenal assessment once biallelic MUTYH variants are confirmed
Monitor for iron-deficiency anaemia and occult gastrointestinal blood loss as possible signals of a missed lesion

Refer for germline genetic testing and counselling when attenuated adenomatous polyposis is identified, especially with a non-dominant inheritance pattern, since MAP is autosomal recessive and both parents warrant testing

Refer to a hereditary colorectal cancer or clinical genetics multidisciplinary service for lifelong surveillance coordination, cascade testing of siblings, and reproductive counselling once biallelic pathogenic MUTYH variants are confirmed
Refer to colorectal surgery when polyp burden becomes endoscopically unmanageable or cancer is found, and to medical oncology for standard-of-stage treatment if invasive cancer is diagnosed
